posts.content:
We received a lot of questions after sharing that Persefoni is now ISO/IEC 42001 certified.

- What does the certification cover? And why did you pursue it?
- Does it apply to a specific AI feature or how to manage AI more broadly?
- What does it mean for customers as we continue adding more AI and agentic capabilities?

The short answer is that ISO/IEC 42001 is about how an organization manages AI.

As capabilities like Analytics Agent, Data Agent, OCR, Smart Emission Factor Matching become a part of the Persefoni platform experience, with more coming very soon, we need consistent processes for assessing risk, assigning accountability, monitoring AI systems, and reviewing how systems change over time.

That same scrutiny is worth applying when evaluating any vendor offering AI or agentic capabilities.

Some questions worth asking:
→ What customer data does the AI need to access, and why?
→ Is customer data used to train models?
→ How is access to that data controlled? And where is it stored?
→ How are AI risks tested and monitored before and after release?
→ Where does human review remain in the process?

AI can take a meaningful amount of manual work of teams' plates. It also introduces new risks that software providers need to account for.

We're grateful for the product, engineering, and IT teams at Persefoni who spend countless (!) hours thinking about these questions and keeping customer data security at the center of how we build.

As our AI capabilities continue to develop, security and responsible AI governance will remain part of the work behind every release. 

You can learn more about what ISO/IEC 42001 means and why it matters here: https://prsfn.ai/4ismo3O

posts.content:
A carbon credit may be certified and still leave important questions unanswered.

A systematic assessment published in Nature Communications (2024) examined 2,346 carbon-crediting projects. Across the project types studied, the researchers estimated that less than 16% of issued credits corresponded to real emissions reductions.

That finding should not be interpreted as evidence that every carbon project fails. It shows why a registry name or certification cannot carry the full weight of due diligence.

Companies still need to ask:
- Would the reduction have happened without credit revenue?
- How was the baseline established?
- How durable is the climate benefit?
- Could emissions simply move somewhere else?
- How will the project be monitored over time?

The credibility of an offset strategy ultimately depends on the underlying project, methodology, and evidence.

Our guide explores different carbon offset programs and the factors businesses should consider when evaluating them: https://prsfn.ai/4fRKgw4

posts.content:
We received a number of questions regarding CARB's June 24, 2026 announcement and its implications for SB 253 compliance. A brief summary follows to help clarify.

CARB has proposed to defer the initial reporting deadline for Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions from August 10, 2026 to November 10, 2026. To effect this change, CARB withdrew its Initial Regulation from review by the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) and has indicated that it will reissue the regulation with limited amendments intended to clarify certain requirements.

Several points warrant emphasis.

1/ The November 10 deadline is proposed rather than final. It remains subject to a 15-day public comment period and to OAL approval before it takes effect. Covered entities should treat it as a working target and not a settled obligation.

2/ The substantive scope of the obligation is unchanged. The revenue threshold (annual revenues exceeding $1 billion) and the "doing business in California" standard remain in place. First-year disclosure continues to address Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, and Scope 3 reporting remains scheduled to begin in 2027.

3/ The deferral is limited in scope. Only the timing of Scope 1 and Scope 2 reporting is affected, together with certain clarifying revisions to the regulatory text. CARB has not yet published the revised regulation or opened the comment period, and has described the forthcoming text only as pending.

Covered companies would be well advised to continue preparing their Scope 1 and Scope 2 inventories notwithstanding the additional time, and to monitor CARB's rulemaking page for publication of the revised regulation and the opening of the comment window.

We've been connecting with a lot of companies over the last few months looking for deeper insights on how to cut through all the AI noise in the sustainability space, and which questions are best to ask when running vendor evaluations.

The questions that separate mature, proven AI functionalities from well-marketed demos are specific and unglamorous. They're about governance, data handling, and whether the vendor can actually explain what their models are doing behind the scenes.

A few worth putting on your list:
1. How do you use AI or machine learning in carbon accounting specifically? (Look for concrete, value-driven features, not just "AI-powered.")
2. Can you explain how your AI arrives at its decisions and what audit trails exist?
3. Which data privacy regulations do you comply with, and are you ISO 42001 certified?
4. What guardrails are in place to detect and prevent misuse or attacks on the AI tool?
5. How do you validate AI inputs and outputs before and after a feature ships?
6. Has your AI undergone independent security audits, and how often?

Vendors who can answer these clearly are the ones worth a second conversation.

posts.content:
Choosing an emission factor can be one of the most judgment-driven steps in carbon accounting. This set of five questions helps keep it consistent:

1/ What footprint source (and scope) am I calculating? This determines which factors and databases apply.

2/ Can I use supplier or activity-specific data? Values that reflect your actual context give the most accurate picture.

3/ What are the primary drivers of emissions here? Different sources behave differently. Electricity is driven by geography; stationary combustion by fuel type; mobile combustion by vehicle, fuel, and distance.

4/ Does the factor align with my temporal and accounting boundaries? Match the year of your activity data and the right method—location- vs. market-based, combustion-only vs. lifecycle.

5/ Is the source credible and methodologically sound? Transparent, regularly updated, peer-reviewed datasets are the most reliable.

Next up, we'll cover the best practices that help keep factor selection rigorous over time.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 3 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Not every emission source demands the same rigor. 

The IPCC tiered framework is a useful way to think about the trade-off. Each tier represents a higher level of methodological sophistication, and therefore lower uncertainty.

→ Tier 1 applies default factors against broad national or global activity data. It's the entry point, and it carries the highest uncertainty.
→ Tier 2 brings in country-specific factors and more granular activity data, reflecting local conditions far more accurately.
→ Tier 3 uses facility-level measurement and process models. Lowest uncertainty, highest effort; reserved for sources where Tier 2 isn't precise enough.

The principle for corporate inventories: apply the highest feasible tier to your most material sources. Global averages are fine for minor spend-based categories. They don't hold up for your largest direct sources, like the fuel you burn on-site or the electricity you purchase, when a region- or country-specific factor is available.

Next in the series: the five questions to ask every time you select a factor.

Earlier this year, on February 26, 2026, the Korea Sustainability Standards Board published the Korean Sustainability Disclosure Standards (KSDS) — two standards closely aligned with IFRS S1 and S2. 

The FSC released a draft implementation roadmap the same day. Under that roadmap, KOSPI-listed companies with consolidated assets above ₩30T KRW (~$20.4B USD) will be required to report Scope 1 and 2 emissions starting in 2028, with Scope 3 deferred to 2031. The next tier of large listed companies begins reporting in 2029.

Korea has joined more than 30 jurisdictions that have partially or fully adopted ISSB-aligned standards. With 2028 closer than it seems, in-scope companies should consider assessing their data infrastructure now.

Our full breakdown of KSDS, including who's in scope, what the standards require, and how to prepare, is linked in the comments. 👇

posts.content:
Not all emission factor databases are created equally. They can vary by geography, methodology, and the type of emissions they are designed to measure.

Geography matters because emissions intensity varies by location. The carbon content of electricity in Washington state looks very different from that of electricity in Texas. A national average obscures that. The same logic applies across countries, which is why regional and country-specific databases exist alongside global ones.

Methodology matters because different databases are built for different purposes. Some are designed for activity-based calculations, such as fuel combustion and electricity consumption. Others are built for spend-based Scope 3 screening, where the starting point is what a company spent rather than what it physically consumed. Using the wrong database for the wrong calculation is one of the more common sources of error in a GHG inventory.

Some of the most widely used include the EPA's Emission Factors Hub, which covers US corporate inventories across Scopes 1, 2, and 3, the IPCC's Emission Factor Database, which is the standard reference for global averages, and the UK's DESNZ, which is the basis for UK corporate accounting. You can see a quick comparison in the table below.

When selecting a database, the most important criteria are transparency, regular updates, and scientific peer review. Those qualities are what give a carbon inventory its credibility when it is time for third-party verification.

ICYMI: CARB releases 2026 SB 253 reporting guidance

Yesterday, CARB released its guidance for SB 253 2026 reporting submittals. The deadline for Scope 1 and Scope 2 is November 10, 2026, assuming OAL approves the Initial Regulation.

The guidance is consistent with the December 2024 Enforcement Notice and leaves flexibility for first-year reporting:

→ Entities can submit an existing annual report, data already reported elsewhere, or CARB's draft template.

→ CARB will accept submissions whether or not limited assurance was obtained.

→ CARB is not prescribing a specific Scope 2 emissions factor dataset for 2026. Companies may use whichever credible source they identify.

→ Companies that were not collecting data as of December 5, 2024 are asked to send a statement of non-reporting on letterhead instead.

→ The intake platform is voluntary this year and can be used for contact information, the report itself, or billing information for fee invoicing.

𝗢𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲: The guidance should make the first SB 253 reporting cycle more manageable for many companies. CARB is allowing organizations to work with emissions information and reporting processes they already have in place rather than prescribing a single format for 2026. Companies should still view this year as an opportunity to establish a repeatable reporting process, particularly as CARB develops more detailed requirements for 2027 and beyond.

The California Air Resources Board (CARB) shared several important updates today on how California’s corporate greenhouse gas reporting requirements are expected to take shape under SB 253.

For 2026, CARB intends to move the first reporting deadline to November 10, pending a forthcoming rulemaking package that will formalize the change and clarify parts of the initial regulation.

Companies would report Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions only, with no assurance required. They may rely on data already in their possession or being collected as of December 2024, rather than beginning new data collection solely to comply in the first year. Additional reporting guidance is expected by September 1.

For 2027, CARB is proposing that companies begin reporting five Scope 3 categories:
• Cat 1: Purchased goods and services
• Cat 3: Fuel- and energy-related activities
• Cat 5: Waste generated in operations
• Cat 6: Business travel
• Cat 7: Employee commuting

The remaining ten categories would be voluntary for now, with no date proposed for making all 15 mandatory.

Other elements under consideration include items such as limited assurance for Scope 1 and Scope 2, more detailed methodology disclosures, and a 5% threshold for determining when prior-year emissions must be recalculated. The proposal would also bring insurance companies into the program beginning in 2027.

These requirements are not yet final. 

CARB expects to publish a full proposal later this fall, followed by a 45-day public comment period. For companies in scope, the immediate priority is preparing for Scope 1 and Scope 2 reporting in November while building readiness for Scope 3 and assurance in 2027.

We'll be sharing a more detailed write-up on this matter in this month's climate policy newsletter. You can sign up here to receive it in your mailbox once it is out: https://prsfn.ai/46y0Egh

posts.content:
Only one in six of the world's largest companies is on track to meet its net-zero goals by 2050.

It's not for lack of effort. Most sustainability teams are working harder than ever. The challenge is where that effort is going.

Seven to eight months of the year, on average, go to preparing disclosures for different regulatory frameworks. CSRD, ISSB, CDP, SB 253, SECR, SBTi. Each one asks for the data differently. Each one has its own deadline. That leaves very little time for the work that actually reduces emissions.

There's a second cost that gets less attention. When climate work only shows up during reporting season, the people who need to help drive emissions reductions stay on the sidelines. Facilities, procurement, finance, operations, and suppliers get a data request once a year, respond, and move on. The relationships that make decarbonization possible never get built.

The companies making real progress are taking a different approach. They've built a small set of core capabilities that meet every framework's needs and support strategic conversations across the business year-round: carbon accounting, target setting, risk and opportunity management, value chain engagement, decarbonization planning, and disclosure.

With that foundation in place, disclosure becomes a natural output of the work rather than the work itself.

How this works in practice: https://prsfn.ai/4tEsn7V
